body: The seven-twelve is sitting outside the station with the doors shut and no announcement, and a man in the second carriage has taken a book out of his bag. He put it there on Sunday, on purpose. He reads to the bottom of the second page, turns his phone over to check the time, checks something else while it is in his hand, then puts it down. He does that eleven more times in twenty-five minutes. When the train moves he is on page four, and if you asked him on the platform what those pages said he could not tell you. He could not tell you what he had been doing instead, either.

Nothing had happened on the phone. No message, no call, nothing urgent and nothing interesting. He was not being interrupted by the world. He was being interrupted by a habit he had brought aboard with him, and it was working perfectly.

Focus is generally filed as a productivity concern, which puts it in the wrong department. It is not a technique for getting more done before lunch. Attention is the raw material of every serious thing a person does, and it is under organised attack.

Consider what actually runs on it. Prayer is sustained attention directed at God, and there is no version of it that is not. Love, once the feelings have done their early work, is in practice sustained attention directed at one person over a long time — which is why the complaint in a failing marriage is so often not cruelty but absence. Work worth doing means holding a problem long enough for it to give something up. Three rooms of a life, all running off one supply. When it thins they thin together, and quietly enough that a person is well into it before noticing.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air. One, HM 376.50, Inspire Focus, is assigned for exactly this and is still in build: the frequency is held, and nothing plays there yet.

Programming for attention is an awkward thing to commit to, because a station built to be worked over is judged by whether it was forgotten. Nothing on it may be clever enough to make somebody look up, and no presenter breaks in to say what the last track was. Every instinct in broadcasting pulls the other way, the whole trade being built on getting noticed, and here success means an hour went past and you could not say what was on. It is worth the discipline for a plain reason. You cannot pray, work or love anybody with an attention span that has been trained to turn over every nine seconds.

That training is not an accident, and it is not a moral failing in the person receiving it. A great many capable people spent years working out how to hold a human eye, and they succeeded. What they built is delivered several hours a day, and the mistake is to assume it stays inside the phone. It does not; the capacity being reshaped is general. The person who can no longer read a page also cannot sit still in a room, and finds that out the first time they try to pray for longer than four minutes and discover their own mind is the noisiest thing in the house.

The band is laid out so a listener can find a register without hunting. The always-on formats sit together in the mainstream stretch — chill, classical, jazz, coffeehouse, study — several of them assigned and in build rather than on air yet, because that stretch is being filled slowly. Learn roughly where things sit and you can move about by feel, which is the skill a real dial teaches and a search box never can.
None of which is an argument for putting music on while you work. It is an argument about what you are training while you do.

Be fair to silence first, because silence is the real discipline and the rest is scaffolding. The traditional practices were attention exercises before they were anything else — fixed hours, long readings, repetition of the same words, deliberate quiet — and they look pointless the moment you assume the goal was the content rather than the capacity. Nobody prayed the same psalm every morning for thirty years to find out what it said. But silence is not available in most rooms — a road outside, a television through a wall, an open-plan office. And a mind trained to expect a new thing every few seconds does not go quiet when the room does. It fills the room itself.
Instrumental music is a poor substitute for silence and a very good substitute for the alternative.

In a flat above a takeaway a boy of seventeen is revising for an exam he has to pass. The extractor fan runs until eleven and the whole flat smells of it. His brother has the television on through the wall. His mother is at work until one. He has tried silence, which the flat does not have, and he has tried the music he likes, which he ends up listening to rather than working under, because he knows every word and his mouth keeps starting them. So he puts on something whose language he cannot read a syllable of and leaves it. It stops being audible in the second hour. When his mother comes in at twenty past one he is asleep on the papers with the light on and the paper done.

Nothing about that was inspiring and he would be embarrassed to be described this way. The part of his mind that goes hunting for stimulus was given something to chew, and the part that does the work was left alone. That is the mechanism, entire.

It has to be said plainly that no station has ever made anybody focus, and one claiming to would be lying. Music does not build attention; repetition builds attention, and repetition is slow and dull and mostly happens on days when nothing seems to improve. Worse, choosing what to put on is an excellent way to avoid starting: twenty minutes of finding the right thing is twenty minutes not worked. And for some people none of this applies, because any music is a second voice in the room.

That dullness is not a flaw in the method. It is the method. A discipline is not a quality some people happen to possess; it is an exercise repeated until a capacity exists where there was not one, and the repetition is meant to be uninteresting. The point of the station is not the station. The point is that you sat down again, at the same hour, stayed while something ordinary played, and did it again the next day when you did not feel like it. What helps you sit down again is worth its place, and is never the achievement.

So attention is a spiritual subject and belongs with the others, not filed under efficiency. What is being lost is not productivity but the capacity for the three things that need a person to stay in one place: prayer, work and love. They are trainable, and they degrade when they are not used. A station cannot supply any of that. It can hold a room steady for an hour while you do, and be exactly the same tomorrow, which is more than most rooms manage.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial, and it is worth knowing they are there before you turn it. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a great deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them. No menu, no queue, nothing to decide before anything starts.

If you want somewhere to begin, begin at HM 329.00 — Israel Inspire. It is on air, it is worship in Hebrew, and unless Hebrew is one of your languages the words cannot compete for the part of your mind you are trying to use, because that part is busy with English and cannot be in two places. That is the whole trick, and any language you do not read would do it. But this one does something a loop of ambient nothing cannot: what plays while you work is not filler. It is praise, in the oldest working language the faith has, going on whether or not you follow it. You get the benefit of not understanding and none of the emptiness.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people reach for, which is how the next one gets built and how a frequency like Inspire Focus gets its turn.

So take this as an invitation rather than a method. Do not read about attention and do not optimise anything, because both are ways of not starting. Put HM 329.00 on tomorrow morning, open the one thing you have been failing to get to, and stay at it for forty minutes without turning anything over. It will be a poor forty minutes. Do it again on Thursday. The book in the bag on the seven-twelve has been there since Sunday, and it is not going to read itself on the platform.
